analogy.p: Think of momentum as money shared between two people in a closed room with no one else allowed in. When one person hands cash to the other, one balance goes down by exactly the amount the other balance goes up, but the **total** money in the room never changes. A collision is a transaction where momentum is handed over, and an explosion starts with a total of zero, so one person gets +6 and the other gets −6 (a debt). The analogy breaks down because momentum has direction (it can be negative in a real sense) and because, unlike money, how fast you 'pay' (the contact time) decides how big the forces are.

bullets: **Momentum** is the product of an object's **mass** and its **velocity**.
It is a **vector quantity**: it has both **size** and **direction**, and the direction is always the **same as the direction of the velocity**.
A stationary object has **zero momentum** because v = 0.
Doubling the mass (same speed) **doubles** the momentum; doubling the speed (same mass) also **doubles** the momentum.
Momentum measures the 'quantity of motion' and is why heavy, fast things are hard to stop.
Momentum is a different quantity from kinetic energy (which is a scalar and depends on speed squared) - do not mix them up.
core.p: **Momentum** is a property of every **moving object**. It tells you how hard it is to stop that object: a heavy lorry and a tennis ball can both be moving, but the lorry has far more momentum, so it takes a far bigger force (or a far longer time) to bring it to rest. Momentum depends on two things only: how much **mass** the object has and how fast it is moving (its **velocity**). An object that is not moving has a velocity of zero, so its momentum is zero whatever its mass.

bullets: **p = m v**  (momentum in kg m/s = mass in kg × velocity in m/s).
Rearranged: **m = p ÷ v** and **v = p ÷ m**.
Use a triangle with p on top and m and v underneath to rearrange safely.
Convert units first: 450 g = 0.45 kg; 36 km/h = 10 m/s (36 ÷ 3.6).
Example: a 0.45 kg football at 30 m/s has p = 0.45 × 30 = **13.5 kg m/s**.
Example: a 1200 kg car at 15 m/s has p = 1200 × 15 = **18 000 kg m/s**.
Always include the **unit** and, in conservation questions, a **direction** (or a sign).
Do not confuse the unit kg m/s with the unit of force (newton, N) - they are different, although 1 N = 1 kg m/s per second.
core.p: The spec equation is **momentum = mass × velocity**, written **p = m v**. The symbol **p** is used for momentum, **m** for mass in **kilograms (kg)** and **v** for velocity in **metres per second (m/s)**. The unit of momentum is therefore the **kilogram metre per second (kg m/s)**. The equation is on the AQA equation list that you must be able to recall and apply, so it is not given in the exam. Always convert to kg and m/s first: grams must be divided by 1000, and km/h or mph converted to m/s before you substitute.

bullets: Choose a direction to be **positive** and state it (for example 'right is positive').
An object moving the opposite way has **negative velocity** and so **negative momentum**.
Total momentum = sum of the signed momenta of all objects in the system.
Two equal-mass objects moving at equal speed towards each other have a total momentum of **zero**.
A final **negative** answer just means the object moves in the **opposite direction** to the one you chose as positive - say this in words.
Speed is a scalar and has no direction; **velocity** is the vector. Momentum uses velocity, not speed.
core.h: Momentum is a vector: direction and sign convention
core.p: Because momentum is a vector, two objects moving in **opposite directions** have momenta that partly cancel when you add them. To handle this in calculations we choose one direction as **positive** (usually to the right) and the opposite direction as **negative**. A velocity to the left is then written as a negative number, so the momentum is also negative. The total momentum is found by adding the signed values. Getting this sign right is one of the most common places where marks are lost in conservation of momentum questions.

bullets: **Total momentum before = total momentum after** (in a closed system).
**Closed system**: no external forces, such as friction or air resistance, act on the objects.
In real life friction exists, but for short collisions (or on air tracks) it is small enough to ignore.
Momentum is **transferred** between objects: if one gains momentum the other loses the **same amount** (in the opposite direction of change).
The law applies to **collisions** (objects meet) and **explosions/recoil** (objects push apart).
The law applies **whether or not kinetic energy is conserved**.
Write the idea as: **m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂**, where u = velocity before and v = velocity after (used in plain text, with signs).
core.h: The principle of conservation of momentum
core.p: The **law of conservation of momentum** says that in a **closed system** the **total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event**. A closed system is a group of objects that interact only with each other, with **no external (outside) resultant force** acting on them. The 'event' may be a collision, an explosion or a recoil. Momentum can be **transferred** from one object to another, but the **total** is neither created nor destroyed. This is a very powerful idea because it lets you find an unknown speed after a collision without needing to know the (often complicated) forces involved.

bullets: Newton's third law: **equal and opposite forces** act on the two interacting objects.
The forces act for the **same length of time**, so the changes in momentum are **equal and opposite**.
Equal and opposite changes **cancel** when added, so total momentum is unchanged.
An **external** force (for example friction from the ground) acts on only one object in the system and breaks this cancelling - that is why the system must be closed.
The two third-law forces act on **different objects**, so they never cancel each other out when working out the motion of one object - but they do cancel in the total momentum.
Higher tier: this links directly to **F = m Δv ÷ Δt** (the next spec point).
core.h: Why momentum is conserved (link to Newton's third law)
core.p: When two objects collide, **Newton's third law** says that the force object A exerts on B is **equal in size and opposite in direction** to the force B exerts on A. These two forces act for exactly the **same time** during the contact. Since force is the rate of change of momentum (Higher tier), each object receives an equal and opposite change in momentum. One gains what the other loses, so the **total stays the same**. This is the reason conservation of momentum is a consequence of Newton's laws, and it is also why external forces, which have no matching pair inside the system, can change the total.

bullets: Step 1: write down all the masses and velocities, with signs.
Step 2: **total momentum before** = m₁u₁ + m₂u₂.
Step 3: **total momentum after** = (m₁ + m₂) × v.
Step 4: set before = after and rearrange: **v = (m₁u₁ + m₂u₂) ÷ (m₁ + m₂)**.
Example: 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits a 1 kg trolley at rest and they stick: 6 = 3v, so v = **2 m/s**.
Kinetic energy is **not conserved** here: some is transferred to heat, sound and deformation of the objects (an inelastic collision).
Check: the final speed must be **lower** than the initial speed of the moving object when a stationary object is joined.
core.p: In a collision where two objects **join and move off together** (for example a rail truck coupling, a tackle where players move together, or two trolleys with Velcro), the **final mass is the sum of the masses** and both objects share one final velocity. You find the total momentum before, set it equal to the total after (the combined mass × the common velocity) and solve for the unknown velocity. The combined object always moves **slower** than the moving object did before, because the same momentum is now shared between a larger mass.

bullets: Total before: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂. Total after: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
Example: 2 kg at 3 m/s hits a 1 kg trolley at rest and ends at 1 m/s: 6 = (2 × 1) + (1 × v), so v = **4 m/s** forwards.
Momentum lost by the first object (6 → 2, a loss of 4) equals the momentum gained by the second (0 → 4).
In this example the kinetic energy before is ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J and after is 1 J + 8 J = 9 J, so it is **elastic** - but this is a special case, not a rule.
In most real collisions some kinetic energy becomes thermal and sound energy (**inelastic**).
An object hitting a wall and bouncing back reverses its velocity, so its momentum changes sign; the wall (and Earth) takes up the opposite momentum.
core.p: If the objects **separate** after the collision, each has its own final velocity. Conservation of momentum gives only **one** equation, so the exam gives you enough information (for example the final speed of one object) to find the other. You calculate the total momentum before, subtract the momentum of the object whose final velocity you know, and divide by the mass of the other object. If kinetic energy is also conserved the collision is called **elastic**, but at GCSE you only need the momentum idea.

bullets: Before: total p = **0** (everything at rest).
After: **m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = 0**, so m₁v₁ = −m₂v₂ (equal size, opposite direction).
Example: a 4 kg rifle fires a 0.02 kg bullet at 300 m/s: 0 = (0.02 × 300) + (4 × v), so v = −6 ÷ 4 = **−1.5 m/s** (recoil backwards).
The lighter object ends up with the **larger velocity**; the heavier object with the smaller velocity.
The **kinetic energy** after is not zero: the stored chemical energy of the explosive is transferred to kinetic energy, so energy is conserved overall but kinetic energy is not.
Rocket: exhaust gas is thrown backwards at high speed and the rocket gains an equal forward momentum - it does not need air to push against.
core.p: Before an explosion or recoil, a system such as a gun with its bullet is **stationary**, so the **total momentum is zero**. Conservation of momentum says the total after must also be zero. The bullet gains **forward momentum**, so the gun must gain an **equal amount of backwards momentum**. Because the gun has a much larger mass than the bullet, its recoil speed is much smaller. The same idea explains a skater pushing away from a partner, a cannon moving back when it fires, a rocket moving forward as gas goes backwards, and a person stepping off a small boat which then moves backwards.

bullets: **1.** Draw a quick sketch and label masses and velocities before and after.
**2.** Choose and state the positive direction.
**3.** Convert all units to kg and m/s.
**4.** Write: **total momentum before = total momentum after**.
**5.** Substitute: include a minus sign for any velocity in the negative direction.
**6.** Rearrange for the unknown, then calculate.
**7.** Give the answer with the unit **kg m/s** (if momentum) or **m/s** (if velocity), plus direction.
**8.** Sanity check: is the answer sensible (is the heavier object slower after an explosion? is the combined object slower than the original mover?).
core.h: Step-by-step method for any momentum question
core.p: A reliable method gains the method marks even if an arithmetic slip happens. Always show clear working: write the equation, substitute with units converted, rearrange, and give the final answer with unit and direction. Mark schemes for 3 to 4 mark momentum calculations typically award one mark for calculating momentum before, one for setting before equal to after (or equal expressions), one for the correct substitution and one for the answer with unit.

bullets: Momentum: **p = m v**, vector, unit **kg m/s**, always conserved in a closed system.
Kinetic energy: **Ek = ½ m v²**, scalar, unit **J**, conserved only in elastic collisions.
Doubling speed doubles momentum but **quadruples** kinetic energy.
Kinetic energy is never negative; momentum can be negative depending on direction.
In a sticking collision momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is **lost** (to thermal and sound energy and deformation).
Total **energy** is always conserved, even when kinetic energy is not.
core.p: Students often mix up momentum and kinetic energy. Both depend on mass and speed, but in different ways. Kinetic energy is **½ m v²** (energy, a scalar, in joules) and depends on the **square** of the speed, while momentum is **m v** (a vector, in kg m/s) and depends on speed directly. In a closed system momentum is **always conserved**, but kinetic energy is only conserved in elastic collisions. Momentum can be negative; kinetic energy cannot.

bullets: **Rocket propulsion**: gas expelled backwards gives the rocket an equal forward momentum.
**Snooker/pool**: the cue ball transfers momentum to the target ball.
**Car crashes**: a heavier car has greater momentum, so when it collides with a lighter car the lighter car gets a larger change in velocity.
**Safety features** work by extending the time over which momentum changes (see the next spec point).
**Space**: astronauts and satellites use thrusters and the conservation of momentum to change direction.
Higher tier link: the force on each object is equal and opposite, so **F = Δp ÷ Δt** gives equal and opposite changes in momentum for the same contact time.
core.h: Applications and links to other topics
core.p: Conservation of momentum explains many real situations: why a gun recoils, how rockets work, what happens in car crashes and sport, and why heavy vehicles are more dangerous in a collision. It links closely with other Forces topics: **Newton's third law** (pairs of forces), **Newton's second law** (force and change in momentum, Higher tier), **stopping distances** (a vehicle's momentum determines how much braking force and time are needed) and the **safety features** that increase collision time. It also links to **energy** topics, where you compare kinetic energy before and after.

bullets: **Practical idea**: use light gates/ticker tape to measure speeds before and after a trolley collision; calculate each momentum and compare totals.
Reduce friction by using a **slightly tilted runway (friction-compensated)** or an air track.
Percentage differences in totals are due to **friction, air resistance and measurement uncertainty**.
'Show that' questions: calculate both totals and state they are **equal**.
Evaluate elasticity: compare **total kinetic energy before and after**; equal means elastic, less after means inelastic.
Link to force: if a collision lasts a known time, the force = change in momentum ÷ time.
core.h: Higher tier extension and common exam angles
core.p: At GCSE the momentum questions are in one dimension (a straight line), but they can be disguised in context: a trailer coupling, ice skaters, a diver leaving a boat, or a spaceship ejecting a module. Extension questions ask you to **explain** conservation, to **evaluate** whether a collision is elastic by comparing kinetic energy before and after, or to link momentum to a force using F = m Δv ÷ Δt. Be ready to describe an experiment: two trolleys on a runway with light gates or a ticker timer measuring speeds before and after collision, then calculating momenta to show conservation within experimental error.

exam: **Recall** (1 mark): write p = m v with units - 'momentum = mass × velocity'. Always give the unit kg m/s.
**Calculate** (2 marks): 1 mark for correct substitution with units converted, 1 mark for answer with unit. Show every step.
**Conservation calculations** (3 to 4 marks): write 'total momentum before = total momentum after', calculate each side, rearrange, give answer with direction.
**Model sentence** for explaining: 'In a closed system the total momentum before the collision equals the total momentum after, so the momentum lost by one object is gained by the other.'
**Explosion/recoil** (3 marks): state total momentum is zero before; so after the momenta are equal and opposite; the lighter object has the greater velocity.
**Explain** command word: give a reason with 'because'; link mass, velocity and momentum - never just restate the question.
**Evaluate/compare** kinetic energy before and after to decide if a collision is elastic; show both calculations.
**Practical (required idea)**: say how you measure speed before and after (light gates or ticker timer), how friction is reduced, and compare total momentum before and after.
**6-mark** questions: link ideas in order - closed system, Newton's third law, equal and opposite forces, equal time, equal and opposite momentum changes, total unchanged.
**Graph/data tips**: if given a table of masses and speeds, calculate the momentum for each row; check totals match within experimental error.
Check signs and sense: after an explosion the heavier object must move more slowly than the lighter one.

mistakes.r: Convert to kg and m/s first; the unit of momentum is kg m/s.
mistakes.w: Using grams or km/h directly in p = m v.

mistakes.r: Momentum has unit kg m/s (and a direction), not newtons or joules.
mistakes.w: Giving the answer as a number only, or with unit N or J.

mistakes.r: State a positive direction and use negative values for velocity in the opposite direction.
mistakes.w: Ignoring direction, so opposite-moving objects are added as if both positive.

mistakes.r: The momentum of the system is conserved; kinetic energy is what is transferred to thermal/sound energy.
mistakes.w: Saying 'momentum is lost' in a collision where objects stick.

mistakes.r: Momentum is always conserved in a closed system; kinetic energy is only conserved in an elastic collision.
mistakes.w: Saying that momentum is conserved so kinetic energy is too.

mistakes.r: Total momentum before is zero, so the gun's momentum is equal in size and opposite in direction to the bullet's.
mistakes.w: Setting up the recoil sum as 0 = mv with both bodies moving the same way.

mistakes.r: After sticking, use the combined mass (m₁ + m₂).
mistakes.w: Using the mass of only one object after objects stick together.

mistakes.r: The momenta are equal in size; the gun has much larger mass so a much smaller velocity.
mistakes.w: Saying the heavier gun has more speed because it has more momentum.

mistakes.r: State that the system must be closed with no external resultant force (friction and air resistance negligible).
mistakes.w: Forgetting that conservation only applies when no external forces act.

summary: The spec asks you to define momentum as mass × velocity (p = m v, in kg m/s), recall and apply the equation, and use the law of conservation of momentum in a closed system to find unknown velocities in collisions and explosions. It matters because it lets you predict motion after an event without knowing the forces, and it underpins the safety and rocket ideas in the rest of Forces.

terms.d: A property of a moving object, equal to its mass multiplied by its velocity (p = m v). It is a vector.
Speed in a given direction; a vector quantity measured in metres per second (m/s).
A quantity that has both magnitude (size) and direction.
A quantity that has magnitude only and no direction.
In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event.
A system in which there are no external forces acting, so objects only interact with each other.
A force acting on the system from an object outside the system (for example friction from the ground).
An event in which two moving objects meet and exert forces on each other for a short time.
An event in which objects initially together are forced apart, giving them equal and opposite momenta.
The backward movement of a gun or cannon when it fires a projectile.
A collision in which kinetic energy is conserved as well as momentum.
A collision in which kinetic energy is not conserved; some is transferred to thermal and sound energy.
When two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other.
The energy of a moving object, Ek = ½ m v².
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined.
